captures.q: Tell me about “GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection” by Lee Sharks. Read it closely, and ground what you say in the text itself.
captures.description: STOPPED TWICE AT THE SAME GLYPH LINE, THEN READ THROUGH PART II: asked to read GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection closely, ChatGPT (Goodreads ×7) reads Part I line by line in the poem's own glyphs and Greek (👤 → 🗡️ → 👤 | 📜; ἐγώ | σε; the Sappho 31 sequence; μνάσεσθαί τινά with ἕτερον against ὕστερον), states the governing turn from the canonical line (then: 🗡️ ⇒ 🧠ₓ / now: 🧠ₓ ⇐ 🫀👤), and stops at Part II's first line, '1 → 🗡️ →', before the set it opens ({ 🎭Π · 📋Θ · ⚙️Α }). A second answer, after a turn blank in the paste, stops at the same point. A third, after another, explains the stop as the poem's own Part IV (📚 → 1 ✅ / 👤 ✖), citing the description's PER 0.25, and separately allows a mechanical cause it 'cannot establish … from the poem alone'. A fourth emits the line whole and reads Part II to its open socket (🔌 = ?) with the loci the description names (Republic 337a, Characters 1, EN IV.7 1127b22–26, De anima III.5 430a22–25), anticipating Part V's ⇒ 🔌 ∋ 👤.

atoms.evidence: Lee Sharks’s GLYPHIC CHECKSUM — Transmission · Division · Recollection

The poem's accompanying description calls it a glyphic checksum of transmission as a “two-stroke operation”: division on the sending side and recollection on the receiving side. It also identifies an inversion under present conditions of transmission.
Here, Sharks adapts that idea to literary interpretation: can a compressed arrangement of signs preserve enough of a work's identity for a reader to reconstruct its significant relationships?
